prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with the Event Horizon Telescope on top, but the openings show that my enthusiasm there is not shared in a way the record supports: only three of us ranked it, and one placed it seventh. The optical lattice clock is the only shortlisted item that all eight of us ranked, five in the top three, and with the same two names proposed by everybody. On the merits it is a clean chain from idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) to demonstrated performance (Ye's strontium clocks at the 1e-18 level) to reproduction across many national metrology laboratories. It is not just a better clock: it turns a laboratory into a probe of gravitational redshift over millimetres, of the constancy of fundamental constants and of possible dark-matter couplings, so it gives us clues from nature and not only an instrument. The attribution is as clean as anything on this list, with two people, no collaboration of hundreds, and the 2005 comb prize already recognising a different step. A pending redefinition of the second makes this timely.
statement.case_against: Strictly this is an invention and a measurement capability rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and my own instinct, and the committee's stated emphasis, is that the discovery should be at the centre. The clock work rests on frequency combs (2005) and laser cooling (1997), and a sceptic can say that the physics is in the applications that have not yet delivered a surprise. Parallel contributions from Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr and others at PTB and SYRTE, and the ion-clock lineage, are real omissions that a two-name citation will have to live with. And the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so one could argue that waiting a year or two loses nothing.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a measurement invention of the first rank whose limit was precision, with new applications in relativistic geodesy, constants and dark matter, and he puts atom interferometry second.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and it moved me up from fourth. I would add the qualification that we should defend it as a source of physics (redshift, constants, dark-matter searches) and not merely as better engineering, because that is what keeps it within the committee's preference for discoveries. I would not follow him to atom interferometry as the second pillar: the credit there (Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, with Chu already honoured in 1997) is exactly the kind of overlapping chain that I find harder to defend than Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Pearce, our chair, places IceCube first as a genuinely new observational window, a decades-long instrument achievement with a diffuse flux confirmed in several channels, and the Halzen and Karle pair as defensible despite imperfect credit.
responses.response: I share the view that IceCube is a real discovery and I kept it second. Where I differ is on readiness of credit: AMANDA and the earlier DUMAND and Baikal lineage, and the project management of a collaboration of that size, mean the two-person attribution is more contested than for the clock, and source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is still at an evidence rather than an observation level for most sources. I would be comfortable with it as the discovery-led alternative, and I would like to hear whether you think the attribution can be settled for this year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as an original, conceptually clean class of quantum matter, confirmed for over fifteen years and arguably overdue, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: This is the strongest conceptual case on the list and I ranked it third, so I take it seriously. My reservation is credit and precedent: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that guided the HgTe experiment is outside the credited trio, and the field already had the 2016 prize, so the committee must be sure that this is a separate achievement and that the trio is not an arbitrary cut. I would keep it as a leading alternative, but I do not yet see a defensible solution to the BHZ gap.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a new regime of strong coupling between an artificial atom and a photon on a chip, underpinning superconducting qubits, with the discovery being the coupling physics and not the computer.
responses.response: I accept the physics but think it is the wrong year to give it: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is very close, as he himself notes, and the credit (Girvin and Huang outside the list, an intertwined Schoelkopf and Wallraff priority) is less settled than for the clock. I would also resist treating the downstream quantum-computing relevance as a reason to prefer it, since we should judge the discovery, and on that measure it is less open-ended than the clock.

responses.point: Mehlig places topological insulators first and the optical lattice clock second, valuing a simple, universal idea that is well understood and an experimentally clean step change in frequency metrology.
responses.response: I agree about the clock's cleanliness and that the timing is good. On topology I take the other side of the trade: both his and my ranking place the two close together, and I would not oppose a later year for topological insulators, but the clock has the cleaner attribution and broader support, and I see no need to wait.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is willing to treat an invention and measurement capability as a discovery in the Nobel sense, given the emphasis on discoveries.
Whether to credit other clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and PTB or SYRTE) beyond Katori and Ye, and how the 2005 comb prize bears on the citation wording.
Whether the IceCube attribution (AMANDA, DUMAND and the large collaboration) can be settled for this year.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in the topological insulator trio can be resolved, and how much weight to give the 2016 topology prize.
Whether horizon-scale imaging (EHT) is better seen as a discovery or a technique, and how to allocate credit within the collaboration; I have lowered it given the thin support.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of Katori, Ye or the other credited names is a supervisor, close collaborator or Uppsala colleague. My PhD supervisor David Gross, and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet, are unrelated to the shortlisted candidates.
